name: Jump rope
lead: A jump rope, or skipping rope, is a cord with a handle at each end that is swung under the feet and over the head while the user jumps. It is used recreationally, in fitness programmes, in combat-sport training and in organised competition, with freestyle and speed events overseen internationally by the International Jump Rope Union [1].

Skipping is classed as aerobic exercise comparable to running or cycling at moderate to vigorous intensity [1]. It is inexpensive and portable, and in looksmaxxing and fitness communities it is associated with conditioning, calf endurance and staying lean.

A 2022 systematic review and meta-analysis of 21 trials involving 1,021 mostly young participants reported improvements in resting heart rate, body mass index, fat mass, cardiorespiratory endurance, strength, jumping, range of motion and sprinting, with no significant effects on blood pressure, waist-hip circumference, bone or lean mass [2]. Most participants in this research were younger than 18, so the findings do not directly describe adult physique outcomes [2].

paras: Speed ropes use a thin vinyl cord or wire and are intended for fast jumping and double-unders, and they wear quickly on rough surfaces such as concrete [1]. Licorice ropes are made from flexible vinyl or PVC and are common in freestyle [1]. Beaded ropes produce audible feedback when the beads strike the floor and are used in rhythmic skipping and double Dutch [1]. Leather ropes are thicker, less prone to tangling and wear more slowly outdoors [1]. Weighted ropes increase resistance, and with it difficulty [1].

Rope jumping has a long and multicultural history. Wikipedia reports evidence from Han-dynasty China, where stone sculptures depict it and it is linked to a New Year game, and from ancient Egypt, where children are depicted jumping over vines.[1] Explorers recorded vine-jumping among Indigenous Australians in the 16th century.[1] In Europe and North America it was initially mostly a boys' activity in the 16th and 17th centuries and became popular among girls from the 18th century, often with chants.[1] In the mid-20th century the folklorist Lucy Nulton documented American jump-rope rhymes.[1]

In the 20th century it became a staple of boxing and combat-sport training, and Grokipedia names Jack Dempsey among 1920s boxers who used it for footwork and conditioning.[3] Grokipedia also reports that the American Heart Association's Jump Rope for Heart programme launched in 1978 and the American Double Dutch League was founded in 1974, though that page is internally inconsistent in places and its details are unconfirmed.[3] Skipping gained popularity as a space-efficient home workout during the COVID-19 pandemic.[1]

Repeated low jumps load the calves, feet and lower legs rhythmically, raise heart rate quickly, and require coordination between hands and feet [1]. A study published in Gait & Posture in 2019, cited by Wikipedia, reported that skipping produced lower knee contact forces than running [1]. A 2014 study examined whether jump-rope work could serve as stretch-shortening cycle training [4], and a 2020 study in endurance runners linked jump-rope training to better 3-km time-trial performance through greater lower-limb reactivity and foot-arch stiffness [5].

Grokipedia cites a study of skipping versus running in which knee contact forces were lower for skipping; Wikipedia adds that the same 2019 study found about 30% higher metabolic cost.[1][3] A study of jump rope training in preadolescent soccer players examined balance and motor coordination.[13]

Wikipedia lists a progression of skills: the basic two-foot jump, alternate-foot or speed step, side swing, criss-cross, the EB or sailor, and the double under, in which the rope passes twice per jump, with triple and quad unders attempted in competition.[1] The boxer jump uses a staggered stance with weight shifting between feet, giving the back leg brief rest.[1] Partner and group forms include double Dutch and the Chinese wheel.[1]

Rope sizing is commonly done by standing on the midpoint, with handles reaching roughly lower to mid-chest, according to Grokipedia, and typical adult ropes run about 8 to 9 feet; handles often use ball-bearing swivels to reduce tangling.[3] Good form is described as soft knees, landing on the balls of the feet and turning the rope with the wrists.[3]

The 2022 meta-analysis of jump rope training lasting 6 to 40 weeks reported effect sizes from small to large on fitness outcomes in healthy young participants [2]. A 2023 meta-analysis of 15 studies in 10- to 12-year-olds found that jumping rope did not show a significant advantage over regular physical education for body morphology, while reporting subgroup improvements in fitness measures such as speed, strength and endurance in boys and resting heart rate in girls [6].
Evidence for calf size specifically is limited. The studies above measure endurance, jumping and body composition, and did not report calf muscle growth as an outcome in the abstracts available.

The International Jump Rope Union, formed by the merger of earlier federations, received observer status from the international sports federation body GAISF in 2018; its first world championship was in Colorado in 2023 and its second in Kawasaki, Japan, in 2025.[1] Events are judged on difficulty, execution, synchronisation for teams, and speed.[1] A US federation formed in 1995 and was later renamed USA Jump Rope.[1] Grokipedia reports that skipping was demonstrated at the 2024 Paris Games and that advocates are targeting the 2032 Brisbane Olympics.[3]

Overuse injuries of the calf, shin and Achilles tendon are commonly reported among beginners who increase volume quickly, and repeated landings on hard surfaces load the joints.[3] Grokipedia says shin splints and joint strain are common with poor form or rapid progression, that people around 100 kg or more face greater joint load, and recommends warming up, gradual progression, supportive shoes, softer surfaces and strengthening of the calves and ankles; it mentions one comparative study with higher injury and dropout rates in a skipping group than a jogging group.[3] A study of footwear selection for jump rope examined how different shoes change lower-extremity biomechanics.[7] Skipping produced lower knee joint forces than running in a 2019 study.[1]

A 2022 meta-analysis pooled 21 trials in healthy young participants [2], and a 2023 meta-analysis pooled 15 trials in preadolescents [6]. In a 2025 randomized trial of 120 overweight or obese adolescents aged 10 to 13, a 12-week interval jump rope programme in physical education was tested against no training for body composition, fitness and glycolipid metabolism [8]. Smaller randomized trials in obese adolescent girls and boys have examined body composition and insulin sensitivity after 12 weeks of jump rope exercise [9][10], and a trial in adolescent girls with prehypertension examined abdominal adiposity and vascular function [11]. Trials in athletes include an 8-week combined jump-rope and elastic-band programme in young basketball players, which improved agility, balance and sprint times [12]. Adult-specific trials focused on appearance outcomes were not found.

In appearance-focused communities, jump rope is discussed as a cheap conditioning tool for staying lean and training footwork and calf endurance. Online communities dedicated to jump rope, such as the r/jumprope subreddit, focus on technique, rope selection and freestyle skills. Weight-bearing jumping is also mentioned for bone density, with Grokipedia citing a study of heel bone density in pubertal girls.[3]

A more fringe idea on looksmax.org pairs jump rope with blood-flow restriction and spinal decompression as a way to gain height; its author claims it deposits bone mineral around microfractures. No published study has tested such a protocol, and the 2022 meta-analysis found no significant effect of jump rope training on bone in young participants.[2]

lore.intro: On fitness and looksmaxxing forums jump rope is a cheap cardio and calf-conditioning tool, with some fringe height claims attached.

claims.claim: Skipping keeps you lean and athletic
claims.believers: Boxers and lifters use it as high-intensity cardio and a finisher; it is cheap and fits a small space.[1][3]
claims.experts: A 2022 meta-analysis of 21 trials in young people reported improvements in BMI, fat mass and cardiorespiratory endurance.[2]

claims.believers: Many trainees say daily skipping conditions and shapes the calves.
claims.experts: Trial abstracts report endurance, jumping and body-composition outcomes rather than calf size.[2][5]

claims.claim: Jump rope plus blood-flow restriction and decompression adds 2-4 inches of height
claims.believers: The author of a looksmax.org guide says restricting blood flow and impact loading create microfractures that mineralise.
claims.experts: No published study has tested this; the 2022 meta-analysis reported no significant effect on bone in young participants.[2]

claims.claim: Skipping is easier on joints than running
claims.believers: Boxing coaches present it as a low-cost conditioning staple.[3]
claims.experts: A 2019 Gait & Posture study reported lower knee contact forces than running, with higher metabolic cost; Grokipedia also cites a study with higher injury rates in skipping than jogging.[1][3]

angle.text: Jump rope is used as cheap, portable cardio to stay lean and to train footwork and calf endurance. Appearance gains come through fat loss and conditioning rather than a direct cosmetic effect.
